poems:
If it's a weekday a bell closes the exchange somewhere.
Everywhere else, a chair pushed back on purpose.

4:01. A calendar reminder snoozed
with real hatred.
Gym lot: eleven cars, nine still running.
The teacher stays. The room keeps the smell of pencil shavings and orange peel.

Due today:
the report,
the milk,
an apology.
Everyone agrees to take it offline. Nobody takes it anywhere.
Somebody's grandmother is eating dinner right now and considers this normal.
At 4:07 the copier jams and somebody with a master's degree kneels in front of it.

4:08. The school zone light stops flashing.
Traffic resumes its personality.

Your back and the chair have history.
It goes back to two o'clock.

“I'm going to hop off, I've got a hard stop.”
Nobody has ever had a soft stop.
Bus 41 pulls away with one kid asleep against the glass.

Every kitchen on this street is about to have
the same argument about dinner.
The gym at 4:13: three treadmills, one conversation about a boat.

Preheat to 375.
The casserole is for the neighbors.
The reason is nobody's business.
The lot begins its slow leak.
4:16. Two people in a stairwell, one of them crying, both agreeing it is allergies.
A UPS truck double-parked with the engine off, which means he is close.

4:18. A prescription rattles its yes
into a white bag, stapled shut.

Half a sandwich in the break room fridge with a name on it in Sharpie.
The name is a lie.
Quitting time (n.): a number two people in the same building will not agree on.
He leaves at 4:21 every day and has never once been asked why.
Onions bought, not yet cut.
The dog heard a car door. The dog is wrong.
An expired tube of sunscreen on the sill, kept for reasons.
Pickup is at 4:30. You left at 4:00. You are ninth in line.
A hospital hallway. A cart with one wheel that argues.
The bar props its front door open. Two men are already sitting where they sit.

Text: on my way.
Location: the desk.
One minute left in the meeting and the person who has said nothing raises a hand.
Half past. Tea in England, the second cigarette, a stapler being used with feeling.
The crew left at three. Their sawhorses stand in the road like they mean it.
A cat asleep in a laundry basket.
Warehouse floor. He counts down not the hours but the pallets.
4:34, and the printer is out of magenta, a color nobody here has ever asked for.
You could still salvage today. Twenty-five minutes of it, anyway.
An open bag of pretzels, folded once, badly.
Somewhere a school gym is a polling place, a food bank, a wedding. Not today. Today it is a school gym.

4:38. The inbox answers itself in one burst,
fueled by the will to leave.
Coffee made now is a decision about tonight.
Twenty to five. The email you have been avoiding gets answered in nine words, none of them true.
The dishwasher is loaded wrong and will stay that way until somebody else's evening.
Wet hair in the gym lot, February or July, driving home with the heat on or the air on.

Sign on the register: BE BACK IN 5.
The 5 does not say since when.
The afternoon's last honest hour was spent hours ago. This is what came back.
Quarter to. Somebody's alarm goes off for a shift that starts at five.
A retiree at the hardware store buying one screw. He is in no hurry and he is correct.
At 4:47 the ice machine delivers, all at once, everything it has been working on.
Homework is on the table. Homework has been on the table since 3:30.
Happy hour prices posted in chalk, unchanged since the chalk.
Ten to five. The good ones start looking busy. The great ones started at four.
Water on early, out of hope.
4:52. Nobody has ever scheduled anything at 4:52. This minute has never been asked to do a thing.
The last kid at pickup, backpack on both shoulders, standing.
Instructions for the next six minutes: none. There will be no test.
Five to. Someone hits send, then stands, in that order, both quickly.
Aprons going on somewhere. Sleeves rolled. Two cooks in a walk-in, not talking, counting.
Your keys have been in your hand for three minutes.
The hour has done what it does. Two minutes of it are still owed to somebody.
4:59, which is not five, and everyone in the building knows the difference.
